Posted January 3, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: This is one of the most moving testimonials that I have ever received. The first item here is from the patient’s father. The second is from the son. He is obviously a remarkably talented and courageous young man. Thank God that he is now doing well.)

Mr. Cowan:
I must write privately, but want you to know that your work and information provided massive help for my now 17-year old son.

In March 1999, he was 15 and was found to have cancer, a bone tumor called osteosarcoma, in his leg. He had over 172 nights in the hospital and 22 rounds of chemo (3 types in rotation) and a bone transplant. So far, so good, now a year later. His scans are clear; unfortunately, he can't move his left foot (infections after bone transplant, surgeries, et al), but is fine otherwise.

We baked brownies together (not the bonding one normally wants, for sure!) and he dosed one every two hours during most of his chemo rounds.
See
My Problem and how I solved it, " I broke the law to save my son. "

The times he did not add this to his medicine, the chemo caused great pain and sickness. He was also on Marinol (which he didn't like nor think as useful) and another drug (which cost us $26 per pill).

My son figured once that he could have saved his insurance company about $4,000. a month if they had just provided medical weed, instead of the other two drugs.

Doses by inhaling was much, much easier than the round Marinol pills, which are very hard to take when you are throwing up.
See
Marinol Was The First Schedule 2 Drug To Be " Down-Scheduled, "
Boasts Roxanne On Its New Marinol.com Web Site.
Doesn’t That Mean That It Should Never Have Been Schedule 2 Anyway?
and links

Stay at it, Mr. Cowan. It matters. Thank you.

By the way, the hospital staff turned their heads and ignored my son's use of the brownies, etc. They know it works. (They also know that kids break ribs from throwing up from chemo.) He also shared with others on his Pediatric Oncology Unit. It is a sad secret that we are forced to hide this help.

I don't wish cancer on anyone, but if those against medical marijuana ever had chemo, they would surely understand.

It was also an odd moment when my son heard that our state was considering a medical marijuana law --with an 18-year old limit.

" Outlaw cancer for kids under 18 " was my son's reaction.

He will, no doubt, be active forever in the movement to change the laws. Right now, he just wants to be 'normal' again.

Best wishes, in private please,
G

My son wrote this--not bad--for school in August 1999, during his chemo. Thought it might be useful--he ws 15 at the time--since it is first-hand and real.

Best wishes. G

" Bill chose not to inhale, I'd like the same choice. " By J at age 15.
(MarijuanaNews note: Notice that in his school essay the son could not mention having used medical marijuana.)

Cancer. Have you ever thought about having it? Ever considered chemotherapy? Losing all your hair and vomiting until you black out because your anti-nausea drugs just don't work? Well, if you're like most people, you probably haven't. I certainly never did until March 23, 1999. That's the day I was diagnosed with osteosarcoma, or bone cancer.

Before I go on, let me introduce myself. My name is J--- and I am 15 years old. I have a highly aggressive bone cancer, which requires months of inpatient chemotherapy and a lot of surgery. Before my diagnosis, I was pretty much your average teenager. I spent my time hanging out with my friends and my girlfriend. I loved going to concerts of all kinds, especially Boston punk rock and techno raves. At home I liked to write poetry, draw and watch TV and movies. I played everything from basketball and football to frisbee and hackey sack. I loved skateboarding and snowboarding.

But since beginning my treatment, my life has taken a 180 degree turn. I had to leave school in the third quarter of my freshman year. I had to quit playing all of my sports. Now, on my better days, I've started having tutoring so I can finish ninth grade and start tenth. But I spend more time in the hospital than I do at home. And you know what I've found out? Chemotherapy is the most disgustingly evil thing in this world.

Chemotherapy can come in pill or IV form. Because my cancer is so aggressive, the chemotherapy I get is extremely aggressive as well. My chemo consists of three different liquid chemicals that I receive through a permanent IV in my chest. Chemotherapy is part of the most effective way to combat my kind of cancer, but it is unbelievably harsh. My hair fell out. I lost 25 pounds. And that was the easy part.

Some of the dangers of my chemo drugs - cisplatinum, doxorubicin and methotrexate - include hearing loss, eyesight loss or impairment, damage to my heart, liver, kidneys and bone marrow, and secondary cancers. Scary that chemotherapy can actually cause cancer. Then there are mouth sores. They cover the whole inside of my mouth and sometimes down my throat. They stop me from eating and drinking and sometimes from even opening my mouth at all.

Basically the chemotherapy chemicals make me feel horrible. I have constant bone pain and headaches. My vision is blurry. I am always exhausted. But the absolute worst is the nausea that I live with night and day. When I come into the hospital for chemo, I'm in for between five and seven days at a time. And every day of a chemo session, I vomit. Not just your average puke, but painful power puking that is so violent I've heard of other people cracking ribs in the process. And some of my chemo drugs can make me vomit for up to a week or more after a treatment. Sometimes just looking at the chemo liquid (which is so toxic it can't come in contact with bare skin, even though it flows right into my bloodstream), will make me puke.

In fact, just trying to describe the effects of chemo has caused me to boot everything I've ingested all day today.

Chemo alone is not enough to treat osteosarcoma. I also had to have surgery done to remove the tumor in my leg. During the surgery, my doctors removed 5 inches of my leg bone directly below my knee and replaced it with sterile cadaver bone. This new bone is held in place by 16 pins and 2 steel plates that will be in my leg forever. (Now I have a letter from my doctors explaining my condition that I will have to take along with me when I travel because the steel in my leg will set off airport alarms.) This was closed with 59 staples and even more stitches.

This was supposed to happen during a 7 to 10 day hospital stay in the middle of my chemo treatments. Wrong! After the operation, I got pneumonia. Then I got a staph infection in the incision, which required a second and then a third unexpected surgery. In the second surgery, they did a muscle flap, which means they cut two of my calf muscles and wrapped them around my leg to my shin to strengthen the site of the allograft (the bone they put in). Then they stitched the muscles down on the left side of my leg and covered it all up with a skin graft with skin taken from my right thigh. A week later, they found some dead tissue in my leg which, when removed, left a hole in my shin the size of a golf ball. So that meant a third operation, another muscle flap in which they took part of my third and last remaining calf muscle and did another skin graft. They tell me that this third surgery will permanently impair my leg function, but I'm determined to do a lot of physical therapy and work hard at building up the part of the muscle that is left.

The good news is that it has taken three surgeries and 39 days, but I get to go home tomorrow. These surgeries have kept me out of chemo for longer than my doctors wanted, though, so in three days I'll come back and start my chemo again.

I have 11 more chemo sessions to go. My leg is in a cast from just below my hip to down to my toes. Once my chemo is done - hopefully in December or January - I'll be able to return to school. For the next year, I will be in a wheelchair and then on crutches.

All I really want is to be normal and go to school and hang out and not have to think about this stuff. But that's not going to happen for a while. Even when I'm not having a chemo session or an operation, I have a lot of pain and nausea. I'm on five anti-emetics, which are anti-nausea and anti-convulsant medications, plus I've had everything from percoset to valium to dilaudid for pain. But none of these drugs, not even Marinol, marijuana's synthetic relative, completely relieves the pain and sickness.

Marinol is pure THC, made synthetically and then put into pill form. THC is tetrahdrocannabinol, the main active ingredient in marijuana. Marinol was made legal for medical use in 1986 as an anti-nauseant for cancer patients receiving chemotherapy. Its primary goal is the reduction of pain and nausea. Because it is man made in laboratories, it is also medically pure and therefore has no risk of contamination from outside sources. This is good for people undergoing chemotherapy because chemo weakens the immune system and leaves them open to infection and other dangers from foreign contaminants.

However, talking about the benefits of Marinol is all fine and well. If only I could keep it down long enough for it to take effect! Marinol can take between one and four hours to become effective. This happens to be a lot longer than it often stays in my stomach. Marinol only comes in soft gel capsule form, so on days when I need it most, I often puke it up before it can even dissolve. When I do manage to keep it down, it makes me feel edgy and disoriented, which makes things even worse.

During my long hospital stays, I've started reading more about Marinol and the politics behind the medical use of marijuana. One book I've read is called Marijuana Medical Handbook, by Ed Rosenthal, Dale Gieringer and Tod Mikuriya, MD. Based on my own disappointing experiences with Marinol, I'm now starting to think that these authors must be right when they write that " Marinol has proven to be a poor and imperfect substitute for natural marijuana. Though some patients find it useful, many others report that it doesn't work as well as natural marijuana. "

I've read about the Marinol vs. marijuana debate in lots of different books and magazines. I could go on forever about the various arguments for and against each, but I won't. Instead, I will just highlight some of the important points that I have learned.

One is that marijuana is most commonly smoked, and that inhaling it has an immediate effect. So unlike with Marinol, there's no pill to keep down and you don't have to wait for it to be effective.

See
Prohibitionism After the IOM Report; Analysis by Richard Cowan
Repeat After Me: No Medicine Is Smoked! No Medicine Is Smoked! No Medicine Is Smoked! That’s It. You Are Now Qualified To Start Your Very Own Government Funded Anti-Drug Group! Analysis by Richard Cowan
and
Why would anyone want to smoke a medicine? Isn't smoking per se bad for you?

Marijuana is also much less expensive than Marinol.
See
A Medical Marijuana User Says That " Marinol Rescheduling Is Worthless " For Him. He Simply Cannot Afford It. " My country is killing me. "

I'd also like to mention that Marinol consists of THC and THC alone and none of the other cannabinoids found in natural marijuana that may also have potential medical benefits. I will also point out that there are only two major problems posed by the use of natural marijuana for medicinal purposes, both of which have simple solutions.

The first problem is that natural marijuana is illegal. The fight to legalize medical marijuana has made some headway in recent years. In 1996, California and Arizona voted to protect patients from legal persecution for use or possession of marijuana if they had their doctor's recommendation. However, this has not changed the legal status of the drug, and the truth of the matter is that marijuana remains illegal in all of the United States.

The second problem that the medicinal use of natural marijuana poses is that in its unregulated and illegal form, marijuana could contain contaminants that could potentially be harmful to the patient. But if marijuana were legalized, government regulations would see to the elimination of all foreign contaminants, thereby making it both effective and safe.

I am given all kinds of prescriptions - many for expensive drugs that are proven to be highly addictive. But I can't have the one inexpensive, non-addictive, readily-available substance that would make my treatment both more bearable and more effective. Why? Because it is illegal. Why is it illegal? I don't know. Marinol helps me more than anything else, but it doesn't help enough. Medical marijuana could.

All I know right now is that I will spend close to a year of my life being sick and experiencing pain that I wouldn't have to if medical marijuana were legal. I wouldn't have to feel this bad all the time! And I wouldn't have to wait for some new drug to get discovered before I felt better, either. It could be right now. Do you understand? Maybe I could even go to school.

I don't understand why it has to be this way - why you can't have the thing that's there and can help you. And not just teenagers, either. It would help everyone, especially old people whose bodies can't handle a lot of strong drugs. I know if my Grandma were this sick, I'd want to help her. Wouldn't you?

Something has to change.
